The hidden arrow The other day while driving with my 9 year old son we were going through the continuous stream of ‘why do…have you ever thought about…do you think that…’ when one question finally got me. We were following a FedEX delivery van and he asked ‘do you think they fixed the spacing in the letters deliberately to form the arrow to symbolise your packages going from a to b’. At this point I couldn’t have been happier. I had a tangiable example of how he, with ADHD sees the world differently to me (although I’m not claiming only neurodivergent people can see the arrow without being prompted). But I know he is able to see patterns and make connections that I am not and he observes much more these subtleties in life. In every sector shaped by complexity, change, and human consequence, one question matters more than many organisations realise: are we building environments that allow different minds to do their best work? Certainly for my children, I am excited to see how frameworks and technology are leveraged in their school setting to enable them to thrive but what happens beyond school and academia… In January I started to talk with Robert Annis , initially for recommendations on research and courses but, what he has built with his wife Melissa Annis grew to be something I rapidly wanted to be a part of. NEURO is a charity whose mission is bold and timely: turning neuroinclusion into something practical, evidence-based, and structurally real. Not rhetoric. Not tokenism. Real operating change. Providing frameworks and training for organisations and people to enable neurodivergence to be a real strategic and competitive advantage. I’m excited to contribute to that mission and to support its growth across health, life sciences, education, and beyond. If your organisation is serious about innovation, capability, and designing for human difference more intelligently, this is a conversation worth having. www.neurocharity.org #NEUROCharity #Neuroinclusion #CognitiveDiversity #HealthInnovation #Leadership #Education #LifeSciences

Today I’m celebrating my birthday and have a small ask as I think ahead to the London Marathon. And as the miles build, so does the reflection. Marathons have a way of stripping things back to what really matters: consistency, patience, and the ability to keep going. In a world increasingly shaped by instant gratification where quick wins are prioritized, short attention spans dictate content, constant stimulation, there’s something powerful about committing and connecting to something that cannot be rushed. With 42.2 km there are no shortcuts. Being a parent of neurodivergent children has also shaped how I think about resilience, focus, and energy. It’s given me a deeper appreciation for different ways of experiencing the world, building flexibility within routine, the importance of creating space for strengths that don’t always fit conventional systems and as a result being kinder on myself when I don’t get to train or improve as much as I would like. Marathon training, in its own way, mirrors that: learning to work with your mind, not against it. Building structure, staying present, finding ways to keep going even when it’s hard and measuring success differently. And for me, this journey is about more than the finish line. This year, I’m continuing my 50 marathons by 50 challenge in support of Make-A-Wish, a commitment grounded in something bigger. A desire to make a difference for others, a reminder that leadership, at its core, is about service. About showing up not just for your own goals, but for others. I feel incredibly grateful to be healthy enough to be able to continue to push my limits and contribute to something that brings hope to others. So as I step into another year, I’m thinking less about personal milestones and more about life impact. London will be marathon 16/50 and I have 2 more already scheduled for 2026 (Berlin and Luzern) with a few others to be added. If you have a moment today and can spare a £/$/€ to support Make A Wish, my chosen charity, it would definitely boost my stamina and resilience! https://lnkd.in/eZfqFiUD #LondonMarathon #ServantLeadership #MakeAWish #Endurance #Neurodiversity #PurposeDriven #GrowthMindset

International Women’s Day is a moment to celebrate the great women who forged the path ahead of us and indeed those who have shaped our own careers. It’s also a time to celebrate progress. And there has been progress. More women in leadership, more visibility for women’s issues, and greater conversations around equality. But ladies we are far from done! Watching Helen Lambert ’s film Taboo in London this week ( Impatient Health , Women in Pharma (WiP) ) reminded me how much further we still have to go, particularly when it comes to women’s health. Three reflections stayed with me: 1️⃣Women’s symptoms are still too often dismissed. Many women know the experience of being told their pain is ‘normal’, ‘stress’, or that ‘it could be worse,’ or ‘it would be worse if that was the case.’ Delayed diagnoses in conditions like endometriosis, ectopic pregnancies, cardiac disease or autoimmune disease show how frequently women’s voices in healthcare are still not fully heard. 2️⃣ Women’s liberation has not always come with permission for grace. Women have fought hard for equality in careers, leadership, and opportunity. Yet many of us still feel pressure to continue performing at the same pace even during illness, hormonal changes, or chronic conditions to justify the place at the table. Equality should not mean ignoring physiology. 3️⃣ Science needs to change the narrative. Clinical research still often fails to adequately disaggregate sex and gender data. If we studied these differences more rigorously, we might discover something important: treatments could be optimized, safety improved, and in some cases we may even see more favourable outcomes for men and women. Real progress in health innovation will come when we stop treating women as ‘little men’, a variation of the ‘default patient’ and start designing research, medicine, and care that truly reflects biological and lived realities. Awareness is growing - but the next step is action. #InternationalWomensDay #WomensHealth #ClinicalResearch #DigitalHealth

🌟Excellence Is Found in the Details 🌟 Looking back, one of the most formative experiences in my professional life was earning my butler diploma. Professional butler training encompasses many disciplines, including formal service, etiquette, protocol, household management, and the pursuit of excellence in every detail. Yet among all the practical skills, what stayed with me most were the principles behind them. A great butler develops the ability to anticipate needs before they are expressed, remain calm under pressure, pay attention to details others miss, act with dignity, and serve with discretion and professionalism at all times. Those lessons extend far beyond hospitality. They influence how I communicate, build relationships, approach business, and create value for others every day. In many ways, the core principle is simple: Excellence is found in the details that nobody notices—until they are missing. I am especially grateful to Mr. ‚ Rick Fink , Director of the Rick Fink the Butler Valet School in Oxfordshire, for sharing his knowledge, experience, and passion for the profession. His mentorship helped shape my understanding of what true service excellence means. Some lessons stay with us for a lifetime. #Butler #PrivateHousehold #Switzerland #ClientExperience #ServiceExcellence #Leadership #AttentionToDetail #UHNWI #HNWI #ProfessionalDevelopment #Passion #Knowledge #Career

Here's the truth about vacation in my 40s: In my 20’s, I used tanning oil during peak sun time to get ‘an even tan’. In my 40’s, 50+ sunscreen is my best friend and I look like a zebra on the beach. In my 20’s, I spent my time at the beach playing beach tennis or cliff diving. In my 40’s, I absolutely DO NOT leave for the beach without my foldable armchair. In my 20’s, I spent all day on the sand and had a couple of ham sandwiches. In my 40’s, I come back home for lunch, cook a whole chicken and nap for 3 hours. In my 20’s, I loved playing in the pool doing splashy divebombs. In my 40’s, I stand by the pool silently cursing those who do splashy divebombs. In my 20’s, I woke up at 1PM after a night out and went straight to the beach. In my 40’s, I arrive at the beach at 9AM, because I fell asleep on my couch at 9 PM. In my 20’s, I went to a music festival and stayed at the front, right by the speakers. In my 40’s, I stay as far back as I can, close to the burritos, bars and bathrooms. In my 20's, every summer I wanted to meet new people. In my 40's, I want to spend all the time with the friends I have for life. If you’re about to go, I wish you a great vacation! And don’t forget that foldable armchair. It’s a lifesaver.
